Updated assessment: The statement is cautiously positive on real activity (“Job gains have been solid…unemployment…declined substantially”) and notes still-accommodative financial conditions, but it turns clearly hawkish on policy by signaling imminent rate hikes and ending net asset purchases by early March (“expects it will soon be appropriate to raise…”, “continue to reduce…net asset purchases”). 

In terms of the literature: with inflation “well above 2 percent” and a tight labor market, a Taylor-rule lens (FOMC’s 2 percent PCE goal; Federal Reserve implements policy via interest rates) points to policy normalization, which typically tempers risk sentiment. The use of forward guidance to signal the path of the federal funds rate (Fed utilizes forward guidance) and the tapering/cessation of QE (Fed utilizes quantitative easing; QE increases the monetary base) align with evidence that communications about future tightening and balance-sheet runoff raise expected term premia (Cochrane–Piazzesi yield-curve channel) and can weigh on asset valuations even when current conditions look strong. The statement’s emphasis on pandemic-related supply shocks (COVID-19 supply-chain disruptions) frames inflation as partly supply-driven, but the policy response is nonetheless to remove accommodation (consistent with Bernanke–Mihov-style identification of policy tightening when inflation risks rise). 

Netting these elements, the macro tone is mildly positive but the policy stance is hawkish, so overall sentiment is only slightly above neutral.
